content.title: Eternal Sunshine: fifteen fantastic films to remember the late Robert Redford • Journal • A Letterboxd Magazine
content.text: From Wild West outlaws and subversive politicians to aloof heartthrobs and arrogant sportsmen, we look back at some of the Letterboxd community’s favorite Robert Redford ﬁlms. “One of the lions has passed,” Meryl Streep said upon hearing that the inimitable actor, director, producer and undeniable saviors of American independent cinema Robert Redford had died. “Lion” feels like the right word to speak to the actor’s screen presence: powerful, majestic, singular, beguiling and just plain beautiful. You don’t really need anyone or anything else on screen, as long as you have Robert Redford. Nobody that Redford worked with was left unmoved by his talent. His The Way We Were co-star Barbra Streisand called him “one of a kind,” as well as “charismatic, intelligent, intense, always interesting.” Jane Fonda, who played opposite Redford in four wildly different, always compelling movies, said that he “stood for an America we have to keep fighting for.” Indeed, beyond his indelible screen presence as one of the most charismatic leading men we’ve ever had and will ever have, Redford never stopped advocating for independent cinema beyond his own roles. It wasn’t enough to put himself center frame to woo and delight us, to make us forget our daily struggles—he put his money where his mouth was and created change where it was sorely needed. Redford co-founded the Sundance Institute and the Sundance Film Festival in 1978 (during arguably his most prolific and high-profile decade as an actor—others would have just enjoyed the limelight), the seismic impact of which has allowed countless filmmakers to rise up through to today. Martin Scorsese, who Redford directed in Quiz Show, said he “gave the world of American cinema something irreplaceable and lasting with Sundance,” while Ethan Hawke also remembers him as “a fiercely passionate environmentalist.” Redford was all of this and more. His innate charm, humor, rigor and wit as an actor remain unmatched, as does his tenacity and pretty singular optimism that you can, and should, stand up and act on what you believe in once the cameras have stopped rolling. May we honor him by celebrating so many of his sparkling performances (and directorial efforts), many revisited by the Letterboxd community below—and muster up our own courage to keep his fight alive as the world somehow keeps spinning without him. The Candidate (1972) Directed by Michael RitchieWritten by Jeremy Larner “RIP Robert Redford, who could have blankly shown up for movies with that face and voice, but chose instead to showcase a lot of talent and variety in his career. Early as it is, the backroom talks in this film almost feel like a riff on his reputation as difficult and exacting to directors, but he seemed to chill out a lot over the decades. Having a movie like this that's actually good is the icing on the cake for someone who is already one of the great progressive celebrity activists. Losing him in the most politically incoherent month yet of a nightmarish year for American politics feels totemic and shattering.” —Josh Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969) Directed by George Roy HillWritten by William Goldman “I guess there’s a type of comfort thinking about Robert Redford and Paul Newman being reunited now and their lives and legacies being so intertwined forever because of work like this onscreen, but also because of their works off screen. Damn, were they good men. They were smokeshows for sure, but they both consistently used their influence in good and admiral ways and that made them legendary (and even hotter for it!). Rest in Peace to both.” —Lyn All the President’s Men (1976) Directed by Alan J. PakulaWritten by William Goldman, from a novel by Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward “A journalist procedural where chasing down sources in telephone directories and tracing cheques is as exciting as the average car chase in a conventional thriller. Gordon Willis's cinematography is a masterclass in its own right and the late great Robert Redford is excellent as Bob Woodward. He projects a sense of palpable intelligence that compliments and deepens his star charisma. Not many actors could make the act of thinking onscreen as compelling as Redford does here. For all the kudos that he received during his brilliant career, his work here left me thinking that he was probably underrated as an actor. R.I.P.” —Wesley Ordinary People (1980) Directed by Robert RedfordWritten by Alvin Sargent, from a novel by Judith Guest “Watching this so soon after Robert Redford’s passing feels strange, like rediscovering something quietly monumental that never demanded attention in the first place. Redford directs Alvin Sargent’s script with restraint, letting grief and silence speak louder than melodrama ever could. The film digs into depression, guilt, and the ways families fracture when tragedy lingers too long, and it does so with an honesty that feels uncomfortably close to life. What stayed with me wasn’t just the subject matter but the way it unfolds, every pause, every word unsaid between characters becomes heavier than the dialogue itself. It’s a film about ordinary people but also about how ordinary becomes unbearable when love fails to reach through the weight of loss.” —Batman The Old Man and the Gun (2018) Written and directed by David Lowery, from an article by David Grann “Maybe this is an odd choice to pay tribute to Robert Redford, especially considering most of his best works are gathering dust on my watchlist. But upon watching this, I realized it was probably the best way to send off such a legendary figure. It perfectly encapsulates the actor’s appeal and ends things the only way he knew how: on his own terms. Redford had been pulling this stuff for more than fifty years. He brings to vivid life a character of questionable moral judgment and makes him the most magnetic and likable character in the film. Hackers, spies, con artists, and especially thieves are made to look like model citizens as soon as he flashes that mischievous grin of his. No matter who he played, his most dangerous asset was never the gun in his jacket, but his disarming smile and the playful light in his eyes. Many actors and directors today are proving that no one should let life’s obstacles prevent them from pursuing a dream or finding a passion, not even old age. No one exemplified this better than Robert Redford.” —Luke The Way We Were (1973) Directed by Sydney PollackWritten by Arthur Laurents, Francis Ford Coppola “Rewatched this with my mother in honour of Robert Redford since she absolutely adores him and I’m still completely unnerved by what this film makes me feel. I love it, I hate it, I am in awe of it and that’s all there is to cinema in the end—that plethora of emotions becoming overpowering enough to make an impact on you. Farewell, Robert Redford. Thank you for all that you were and did for your art and for the world in general!” —M The Natural (1984) Directed by Barry LevinsonWritten by Roger Towne and Phil Dusenberry, from a novel by Bernard Malamud “Watched in honor of Robert Redford, with two friends who had never seen it. One of my all-time, life-long favorites. The final images hit harder in the immediate wake of Redford's passing - we have lost a legend. The movie is not so much about baseball, but instead is part fable, part myth about talent, weakness, mistakes and redemption. Acting, writing, directing, cinematography, editing, and music are all Oscar-caliber, and the seemingly simple story hides layers of depth and wisdom. The movie's moments of triumph and loss somehow feel suspended in time, captured in amber.” —Mike All Is Lost (2013) Written and directed by J.C. Chandor “Redford was the only one who could have done this. I know he had other more beloved roles, and those roles are as worthy of their accolades as any, but this one stands out to me, especially thinking of Redford at the end of his life. The surrender to death… some even interpret the end to be not a rescue but a hallucination as he drowns, and who knows… but Redford sure lived a hell of a life before he had to surrender. Not an unflawed life, like the old man he made good and bad choices, smart and foolish ones, but he lived… may we all live so strongly, so unwaveringly, so defiantly… and know when it's time to let go. Rest in peace Robert Redford.” —Taliesin82 The Sting (1973) Directed by George Roy HillWritten by David S. Ward “I watched this to honor Robert Redford after his passing on Tuesday. Nobody could play a smooth grifter like him..except, of course, Paul Newman (and those dangerous blue eyes). Together, they’re untouchable. This movie made me feel clever, like I was in on the con from start to finish. The pacing snaps along, two hours gone in a flash. A classic that still feels alive, still pulling the wool over our eyes with style.” —Jake Sneakers (1992) Directed by Phil Alden RobinsonWritten by Walter F. Parkes, Phil Alden Robinson, Lawrence Lasker “This was the film I thought of hearing about Robert Redford’s passing. I know he had more iconic roles, but this role I connected to the most by basically being the most charming dork you’ve ever seen in a film. The ensemble is still insane to think about; a true window into the star power of the late 1980s and early 1990s. It’s still a damn fun blast, effortlessly funny, and thrilling.” —Sergio Barefoot in the Park (1967) Directed by Gene SaksWritten by Neil Simon, from his own play “Robert Redford died and this was the first movie I thought to watch. Cute, typical ’60s bullshit, I just know bisexuals back in the day did NOT play about Fonda-Redford team-ups. Paul don’t you EVER let me catch you slipping again. I honestly can’t even be all that mad at the ‘surrender a bit of your own personality for your husband take care of him make him happy’ horseshit because I, too, would surrender everything and anything for Robert Redford. A little too late for that, but god send me back a couple of decades, I know what to do. Robert Redford. Good old Robbie Red. So much more than just some old actor but at the same time, a blond haired blue eyed white guy. A dime a dozen but also a diamond in the rough. A breath of fresh air and a genuinely handsome star. He’s a drop in the ocean that’s gonna ripple for a long while now.” —Beck Out of Africa (1985) Directed by Sydney PollackWritten by Kurt Luedtke, from work by Karen Blixen, Judith Thurman and Errol Trzebinski “Rest in peace Robert Redford. He was so cool and sexy he overcame how unnatural it is for a grown man to be blonde. With that being said, the scene of him washing Meryl Streep’s hair is engraved in my SOUL.” —ktgesuero Downhill Racer (1969) Directed by Michael RitchieWritten by James Salter, from a novel by Oakley Hall “Rewatched for Redford and Hackman who we lost this year. It’s a lot more slick and artsy than I remembered. Redford’s impact on Hollywood will go down in history as one of the most influential and important in terms of progressing film for the better. He championed good movies, directors and actors and right from the start of his career, this movie is a testament to that. You can trace Tom Cruise's origin story to this movie and Redford as a whole. I think it’s his first really great leading man performance. This is the one that really lets him take charge and show a lot by doing very little and it proves this guy is ridiculously dynamic and striking as an on-screen force all on his own. ” —hessesjoffman Jeremiah Johnson (1972) Directed by Sydney PollackWritten by John Milius and Edward Anhalt, from a novel by Vardis Fisher, and a story by Raymond W. Thorp and Robert Bunker “My father’s favorite Robert Redford movie. When I put the obituary in our family chat, he responded ‘He was a good one. Hope he says hello to Hatchet Jack.’ Beautiful and moving with a minimalist screenplay and maximalist production from Duke Callaghan and Sydney Pollack which taps into something so human within us…the need to connect with the land, and also each other, no matter how hard those needs both can be.” —Andrew The Great Gatsby (1974) Directed by Jack ClaytonWritten by Francis Ford Coppola, from a novel by F. Scott Fitzgerald “RIP Robert Redford. One of the last great movie stars. I wanted to watch a film of his I hadn’t seen before to mark this sad day. He really is the perfect Gatsby—all WASPy good looks and unrequited love. Testament to his star power that he can be the named character, top billed and not turn up till 25 minutes in, and it is still undoubtedly his film.” —AmazingRace321 robert redford retrospective
